summary: A slightly annotated list of the 100 RFCs from RFC 2200 through RFC 2299, giving each one's author, date, title, and abstract. It is a status report on that range, and notes which ones are on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Like a table of contents for a shelf of one hundred documents, with a one-line description of each so you can see what is on the shelf.

questions: what rfcs were published between 2200 and 2299

subtitle: A snapshot of 100 RFCs from January 1999 with their status and abstracts.

tldr.problem: Internet protocols are constantly evolving, and it is useful to have a snapshot of recent RFCs to understand what standards work is happening.
tldr.mechanism: This memo lists the 100 RFCs from RFC 2200 through RFC 2299 with their authors, publication dates, titles, and summaries, noting which ones are on the standards track.
tldr.outcome: It serves as a reference point showing the breadth of work in progress in the IETF circa January 1999, including standards-track and informational RFCs across many areas.

today: RFC 2299 is an Informational RFC that remains unobsoleted. It serves as a historical record of IETF standardization activity from 1998-1999. While the specific status of individual RFCs it mentions may have changed (some have been updated or obsoleted), the document itself remains valid as a reference for that era of Internet standards development.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2299 is an informational memo that catalogs 100 RFCs published between RFC 2200 and RFC 2299 in 1998 and early 1999. Each entry includes the RFC number, author, publication date, title, and a brief summary of the document's contents. The memo also marks which RFCs are on the standards track, indicating which ones define mandatory or recommended protocols.

This type of summary document serves as a historical record and reference guide for the Internet community, showing the scope of work being standardized during a specific time period.
sections.eli5: This RFC is like a library card catalog: it lists 100 other RFCs with a few words about each one, so you can quickly find which RFCs are about what topics.

sections.title: Range and Organization
sections.content:
The 100 RFCs span from RFC 2200 in March 1998 to RFC 2299 in January 1999. They cover an exceptionally broad range of Internet technologies and standards activities, including routing protocols like OSPF and BGP, security mechanisms like TLS and OTP, character sets and internationalization, network management with SNMP version 3, directory services with LDAP, and application protocols.

The entries are presented as a chronological list ordered by RFC number, with each entry containing the RFC number, the author or working group, the publication month and year, the RFC title, and a 1-3 sentence summary describing what the RFC specifies or documents.
sections.eli5: The RFCs listed go from March 1998 to January 1999, covering topics from how routers share maps to how to send secure emails.

sections.title: Standards Track Identification
sections.content:
Many RFCs in this range are on the standards track, marked in this document with [STANDARDS-TRACK]. These RFCs advance through the IETF standardization process: they may be Proposed Standards (fresh proposals), Draft Standards (tested and widely reviewed), or Full Standards (mature, widely implemented, and thoroughly tested). Non-standards-track RFCs are Informational (explaining existing practice or providing reference material), Experimental (describing ideas not ready for standardization), or BCP (Best Current Practices for how the Internet community operates).

The note in the RFC explains that readers should consult the latest edition of the Internet Official Protocol Standards (a separate document) to find the current status of any RFC mentioned, as statuses change during the standards process.
sections.eli5: Some RFCs in the list are marked as standards track, which means they follow a formal process to become official Internet rules. Others are just for information.

sections.title: Notable Protocols and Standards
sections.content:
Several significant protocols appear in this range. RFC 2246 defines TLS 1.0 (Transport Layer Security), the foundation for secure web and email communications. RFC 2251-2275 cover SNMPv3 (Simple Network Management Protocol version 3) with its architecture, security models, and applications. RFCs 2247-2256 define LDAP v3 (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol), the modern directory service standard. RFC 2279 specifies UTF-8, the encoding that allows any Unicode character in plain-text systems. RFC 2329 documents the OSPF routing protocol's advancement to Full Standard. RFC 2283 describes multiprotocol extensions to BGP-4, enabling it to route for IPv6 and other network layers.

These RFCs represent major standardization milestones in security, network management, directory services, internationalization, and routing during this period.
sections.eli5: This list includes some very important RFCs like TLS for secure connections, LDAP for finding people and computers, and UTF-8 for writing in any language.
